messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Binary phenotypes... Why so slow? Solutions?
messages.body_plain:
The normal noise-added model I suggested is a hack, and is intended as a way to get out of the numerical convergence issue.  A genome scan is basically a regression model multiplexed.  In your case, logistic regression is having numerical problems because of sparse counts.  There is something called "exact logistic regression" that is meant for this scenario.  SAS and Stata have implementations, but R only has an approximate version as far as I know.  But using exact logistic regression is not a realistic option, I would think.

If you are using permutation testing, then you can use the noise-added hack to make your pipeline go through.  Make sure that your final conclusions are not too dependent on this choice, however, when you get the final results.  For example, if you end up getting a hit with sparse counts, you should be suspicious.

Saunak

Mehta, Cyrus R. and Patel, Nitin R. (1995), “Exact Logistic Regression: Theory and Examples,” Statistics in Medicine, 14, 2143–2160

Hi Karl and R-QTL users,

I have a question about whether I should drop the markers that with no genotype data.

I have a mouse F2 cross and I use 3 markers on ch16, 10.8cM, 32.0cM and 50cM. The marker at 10.8cM does not work very well and I cannot get clear clusters during SNP analysis. Therefore all the genotypes are NAs at marker 1.  I made two csv files, one has all the markers and the second one does not have the first marker on ch16. When I plot both crosses in R, the length of ch16 from the second csv is much shorter. This makes sense since the first marker is dropped in the second csv.  I also see command "drop.nullmarkers" and it makes me feel that I may need to drop the markers with no genotypes.

However, I only have 3 markers on chr16 which is about 40 cM long from est.map and by dropping first marker, the length of chr16 from est.map is only 20 cM.  Also will by dropping null markers  influence sim.geno results?  With two markers, sim.geno can only fill in the gaps between these two markers but with three markers, although the first one is NAs, sim.geno may also be able to fill the genotypes which is right upstream to marker2? Just guessing

Thanks

Pin

messages.body_plain:
I would omit the markers with no data.

In my experience, QTL inference beyond the terminal typed markers is not trustworthy.

The results of sim.geno, in between the typed markers, will not be affected by whether you include that other untyped marker or not.

karl

messages.body_plain:
I got the following question by email, and I thought others might benefit by the question and my response.

> If I ran the QTL analysis and then closed the window. Is there any way to go back and estimate effects and check additive effect  and use fit qtl with rerunning the entire analysis?

When you close R, it should ask "Save workspace image? [y/n/c]:"

If you respond "y", it will save all of the objects in your workspace, and so they'll be there when you run R the next time.

Within a session, you can use save.image() to save your workspace.

karl

Dear Karl

I have the same question, as already posted in 2009 by the user "Masato". I placed Masato's question as well as your answer from that time bellow.

User "Masato" Question 04/03/2009:
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Hello,

I wonder if I can perform the permutation test of multiple qtl model.
When I scanned the genome with scanone and scantwo, I could not get
any peak over the threshold level (alpha=0.05)  according to my
permutation-test (I used cluster for scantwo.perm).
I picked up a couple of highest peaks which were even blow alpha=0.10,
and builded a multiple qtl model, perform fitqtl, addqtl, addpair,
etc. to refined it.
Then I have got a 8QTLs with 3 interactions model. Each QTL and
interaction are highly significant according to p-value .
My wondering point is whether I can conclude they are "real QTLs"
because I couldn't get any significant peak in my scanone and scantwo
results.
I am hoping I could get the LOD threshold info of alpha=0.05 which I
can apply the result of fitqtl.

The following may not make any sense, but just in the case if it
works.
addcovar and intcovar options in scanone and scantwo seem useful if I
perform permutation tests on each chromosome separately, but I'm not
sure if I can incorporate the epistasis between QTLs outside of the
chromosome I'm scanning.
(my model is y~Q1*Q3+Q2+Q4+Q5*Q6+Q7*Q8. All QTLs are on different
chromosomes. How I can write in addcovar and intcovar when I perform
permutation test on Q2?, and others?)

Or, if there is a better way to think, I really appreciate it if you
would let me know.
Thank you.

Best,
Masato
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Karl answer 05/03/2009
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The p-values provided by fitqtl() are pointwise, and do not adjust for
any genome-scan used to identify the putative QTL.

There is no simple way to use a permutation test in the context of a
multiple-QTL model, particularly in the presence of epistatic
interactions.

addcovar and intcovar in scanone and scantwo concern environmental
covariates and QTL x covariate interactions, respectively.

karl
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
It's a bit complicated to deal, in R/qtl, with an F2 with progenitors that are heterozygous.

You first need to determine phase (in other words, the haplotypes) in the F1 parents.
Think of the F1 parents as AB x CD, then you need to convert the genotypes to 14 possible genotype codes, as follows:

1 = AC
2 = BC
3 = AD
4 = BD
5 = A = AC or AD
6 = B = BC or BD
7 = C = AC or BC
8 = D = AD or BD
9 = AC or BD
10 = AD or BC
11 = not AC
12 = not BC
13 = not AD
14 = not BD

For example, if a SNP were segregating in the first F1 parent but not the second, with the phase ab x aa, then the F2 offspring would be aa and ba, and the codes would be

aa = AC or AD = 5
ab = BC or BD = 6

If the phase were instead ba x aa, then the codes for the F2 offspring would be

aa = BC or BD = 6
ab = AC or AD = 5

karl

Hi all. I recently found this post very useful and figured I would add a point here.
When doing eQTL analysis, you may find that you need to cbind a very large list of scanone objects. For example, R/qtlhot needs a large multi-phenotype scanone object. If you generated scanones using multiple QTL modeling, you would then need to make a single scanone out of many.
Karl's solution below works well for <5000 phenotypes; however, for more phenotypes, it becomes very slow. The work around posted below splits up the task into chucks of scanone objects (default is 100), then binds those objects back together.  This takes <2minutes for 10000 traits, whereas the single scanone approach takes several hours on my machine.
Cheers,
John

Here is the function:

combine.s1<-function(s1s,n=100){
  sets<-split(1:length(s1s), ceiling(seq_along(1:length(s1s))/n))
  cat("combining scanones by sets of", n, "\n")
  out.byset<-list()
  for(i in 1:length(sets)){
    out.byset[[i]]<-s1.test[[sets[[i]][1]]]
    for(j in (min(sets[[i]])+1): max(sets[[i]])){
      out.byset[[i]]<-cbind(out.byset[[i]], s1.test[[j]])
    }
    cat(length(out.byset)*n,"...")
  }
  out.all<-out.byset[[1]]
  cat("\n combining sets (total =",length(s1s),") : \n")
  for(i in 2:length(out.byset))  {
    out.all<-cbind(out.all, out.byset[[i]])
    cat(length(colnames(out.all)),"...")
  }
  return(out.all)
}

messages.body_plain:
You're not alone; interpreting scantwo results can be confusing.

> 1) In the examples and the book, sometimes a 20% significance levels can be used while other times 0.05. How should I decide which siginificant level to choose?

The significance level is a personal choice that depends upon what you're trying to do and how conservative you want to be. For example, are you exploring possible interactions, are you trying to decide whether there could be two QTL in a given region, or are you trying to make firm declarations about whether a pair of loci interact?

When I look at summaries of the results of scantwo (and scanone, for that matter), I would generally be a bit more liberal and use a significance level of 0.20. I want to see the interesting possibilities and not just the things that are strongly supported.

When I'm trying to choose a final multi-QTL model whose components I can believe in, I'll be more conservative (with a significance level of 0.05, say).

> 2) If I choose to use (0.0., 0.05, 0, 0.05, 0.05), Are they correspond to (>) lod.full, lod.fv1, lod.int <http://lod.int>,lod.add, and lod.av1? Ten since I have set the int threshold to 0, how should I know if there's potential interactions?

Yes the five significance levels correspond to ld.full, lod.fv1, lod.int <http://lod.int>, lod.add, and lod.av1, in that order.

Using a threshold of 0 for lod.int <http://lod.int> is saying, basically, ignore lod.int <http://lod.int> completely in picking what chromosome pairs to display. I'd probably still, after that fact, look at the observed lod.int <http://lod.int> value to decide whether there was good evidence for an interaction.

karl
